item.title: JAMA
JAMA Editors' Summary Podcast September 25, 2026
item.description: Listen to the JAMA Editor’s Summary for an overview and discussion of the important articles appearing in JAMA.

item.title: Lipoprotein(a)-Lowering Agent Fails to Reduce Cardiovascular Events
item.description: The experimental drug pelacarsen did not reduce the risk of adverse cardiovascular events in a phase 3 study, despite lowering lipoprotein(a) (Lp[a]) levels, the manufacturer announced.

item.title: FDA Approves Updated COVID-19 Vaccines for 2026-2027
item.description: The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved 4 updated 2026-2027 COVID-19 vaccines formulated against the XFG variant.

item.title: GLP-1 Drugs Not the Most Effective Treatment for Obstructive Sleep Apnea
item.description: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists help treat obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), but the medications work best alongside other therapies, a narrative review found.

item.title: Both High and Low Testosterone Tied to Higher Atrial Fibrillation Risk
item.description: Both low and high testosterone in men may be associated with an increased risk of atrial fibrillation, a review suggests.

item.title: NFL Player Death Records May Underreport Neurodegenerative Disease
item.description: Neurodegenerative disease may be underreported on death certificates of former professional football players, according to a study published in JAMA Network Open. The finds have implications for the general population, the researchers said.

item.title: New Guidance for Common Hair Loss Disorder
item.description: Adults with severe alopecia areata, an autoimmune hair loss disorder that affects more than 7 million people in the US, should primarily be treated with oral Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors, according to a consensus statement published in JAMA Dermatology.

item.title: Which Profession Has the Highest Risk of Radiation-Related Cancer Mortality?
item.description: This Medical News article discusses findings that pilots and flight attendants have a higher risk of death from radiation-related cancers than other professions and examines what the results may mean for occupational protections for aircrew.

item.title: ACOG Strengthens Recommendation for Fallopian Tube Removal to Prevent Ovarian Cancer
item.description: This Medical News article discusses the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists’ clinical practice update on opportunistic salpingectomy procedures to prevent ovarian cancer in patients with average risk.

item.title: Research Letters at JAMA
item.description: Important research findings do not always require a lengthy manuscript. Research Letters in JAMA offer authors an effective way to communicate focused, timely, and impactful studies in a high-profile journal (2025 Journal Impact Factor = 65.4).

item.title: Polypharmacy and Drug-Drug Interactions Among Older Adults
item.description: This study uses a nationally representative sample to estimate changes in the use and concurrent use of prescription and over-the-counter (OTC) medications and dietary supplements among older adults in the US between 2015-2016 and 2021-2023, including use of potentially major drug-drug interactions.

item.title: How ARPA-H Is Rethinking Innovation in Health Care
item.description: JAMA+ AI Associate Editor Yulin Hswen, ScD, MPH, and Bon Ku, MD, MPP, program manager at the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H), discuss what it will take to design AI systems that meaningfully improve health for the JAMA+ AI Conversations podcast.

item.title: Months, Not Years
item.description: In this narrative medicine essay, a newly graduated medical student about to start his orthopedic residency halted his training upon learning his cancer had returned and was inoperable.

item.title: Prediction Utility of Urinary Albumin-Creatinine vs Protein-Creatinine Ratios in Chronic Kidney Disease
item.description: This study compares the clinical utility of the urinary albumin-creatinine ratio (UACR) vs the the urinary protein-creatinine ratio (UPCR) for prediction of kidney failure, chronic kidney disease (CKD) progression, and cardiovascular outcomes in an established CKD cohort.

item.title: Lifestyle Modification and Incretin Therapy for Individuals With Obesity
item.description: To the Editor A recent JAMA Insights article proposed that lifestyle modification be reconceived as an adjunct to incretin-based therapy rather than its foundation, noting that even low-intensity counseling preserves most of the weight loss achieved with semaglutide and tirzepatide. Although this reframing is reasonable for weight reduction, it risks understating when nutritional guidance should be delivered. Pharmacologic suppression of appetite, satiation, and food cravings begins within days of initiation of incretin-based therapy, before many patients have acquired the skills to eat well on substantially diminished oral intake. Counseling that occurs after energy intake reduction is reactive at best; the expertise should be proactive and initiated before therapy is prescribed.

item.title: Lifestyle Modification and Incretin Therapy for Individuals With Obesity—Reply
item.description: In Reply The emphasis of the letter by Dr Glatter and Ms Luciani about our recent JAMA Insights article on lifestyle modification and incretin therapy for obesity is that nutritional education and counseling should be a prerequisite to initiating incretin-based therapy. Consistent with recent obesity pharmacologic standards of care and guidelines, we strongly support combining diet and physical activity (ie, lifestyle) modification with obesity medication to achieve critical improvements in adiposity and health. As we have argued, lifestyle counseling is important for attenuating drug-related gastrointestinal adverse effects; preventing nutritional deficiencies; optimizing body composition and physical and psychological function; treating obesity-related complications; and promoting weight loss maintenance. That is why we assert that lifestyle modification is a critical adjunct to pharmacotherapy.

item.title: Long COVID: The Problem Society Wants to Forget
item.description: Long COVID, including the difficulty in defining it and caring for patients experiencing it, is discussed by JAMA Senior Editor Derek C. Angus, MD, MPH, and E. Wesley Ely, MD, MPH, professor of medicine at Vanderbilt University, for this episode of the Healthy Dialogue podcast.

item.title: The Maternal Mental Health Crisis
item.description: This Viewpoint discusses the maternal mental health crisis in the US, outlining gaps in care and assessing the preparedness of the system to handle severe acute perinatal psychiatric crises.

item.title: Hearing Aids for Mild to Moderate Hearing Loss in Adults
item.description: To the Editor A recent JAMA Insights article provided a timely discussion on the role of over-the-counter (OTC) hearing aids. It had been previously demonstrated that self-fit OTC devices can achieve outcomes comparable to audiologist-fit hearing aids, which is particularly relevant in the current context of changing approaches to hearing aid provision. It is encouraging to see this issue addressed in a high-impact journal, increasing awareness among clinicians and the public.

item.title: Hearing Aids for Mild to Moderate Hearing Loss in Adults—Reply
item.description: In Reply In a letter about our recent Insights article on hearing aids for adults with mild to moderate hearing loss, Dr Kim raises an important point regarding the role of professional involvement, and specifically informational counseling in patients with hearing loss and comorbid chronic tinnitus who pursue OTC amplification.

item.title: Medicare Advantage Enrollment and Access to Kidney Transplant After the 21st Century Cures Act
item.description: This cohort study characterizes differences in transplant access between Medicare Advantage and traditional Medicare beneficiaries with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) during the first 3 years after the 21st Century Cures Act (2021-2023), a period of rapid Medicare Advantage enrollment growth.

item.title: The Dangers of Perverted Appetite
item.description: Abnormalities of appetite involve a considerable variety of peculiarities in food intake. Aversion to food may range in intensity from the ordinary anorexia, or loss of appetite, that is familiar to physicians, to an extreme loathing for food. A recent writer has remarked that bulimia, or increase of appetite, is certainly not abnormal so long as it is a simple demand for increased food, as in convalescence; although it might be described as perverted at the court of the emperor Nero, where decadent diners retired for emesis between courses. The “craving sensation” common in catarrhal gastritis and temporarily relieved by eating, and the similar sensation observed in worm infections in children, we are further reminded, are commonly attributed to irritation of the intestinal tract, without further attempt to relate clinically observed effect with physiologic cause.

item.title: Management Consultant Use by Nonprofit Hospitals
item.description: To the Editor Dr Bruch and colleagues provided an important analysis of management consulting use in nonprofit hospitals, but a critical methodological limitation warrants consideration before their null finding is interpreted as evidence that consultants add no value.

item.title: Management Consultant Use by Nonprofit Hospitals—Reply
item.description: In Reply Difference-in-differences analysis does not require the treated and control groups to be similar preceding the engagement with a management consulting firm. The necessary condition is instead parallel trends—that absent the intervention, the average outcomes for both the treatment and control groups would have followed parallel paths. The parallel trends assumption is not directly testable, as one never observes this counterfactual. However, we did probe its plausibility in eFigure 4 in the article’s Supplement 1, wherein we compared the pretreatment trends for treated and control hospitals. We would share the concern Dr Phillips raises if many of our outcomes indicated clear differential trends prior to treatment. However, we did not observe this. There are some outcome measures that are noisier than others, but we did not see systematic evidence of different trajectories preceding the engagement with management consulting firms.

item.title: Screening for Early-Stage Type 1 Diabetes in Children
item.description: To the Editor A recent article provided the first long-term evidence on presymptomatic type 1 diabetes prevalence and progression in the general pediatric population in Germany. Notably, the progression to clinical type 1 diabetes did not differ significantly based on first-degree family history. Based on their findings, the authors concluded that screening should be expanded “beyond genetically selected populations.” As an editorial in JAMA noted, these findings call for a broader screening approach than the latest American Diabetes Association guidelines, which recommend screening based on family history or genetic risk.

item.title: Screening for Early-Stage Type 1 Diabetes in Children—Reply
item.description: In Reply In their letter, Dr Mital and colleagues highlight the importance of considering screening costs alongside potential savings, citing a recent Canadian study suggesting that the costs of type 1 diabetes screening exceed savings from reductions in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), particularly when screening extends beyond individuals with a family history of type 1 diabetes.

item.description: Just heard. So happy that you can now return to dying at the usual pace, no longer

item.title: The Poetry of Remission (and Recurrence)
item.description: Medicine dislikes doubt, preferring instead to assert definitive diagnoses, prescribe clear treatment plans, and declare worried patients to be in remission. Poetry, in contrast, often delights in ambiguity and uncertainty, which are omnipresent in illness experience regardless of physicians’ assurances. In the poem “Remission,” poetic devices such as elision and irony show how patients must cope with unknowns, even after being pronounced disease-free by their physicians. “So happy that you/can now return to dying/at the usual pace,” the poem’s sardonic voice of authority begins, immediately reminding the reader that a reprieve from mortal illness is no promise of untroubled eternal life. At once an expression of medicine’s power and its pesky limitations, the poem goes on to catalogue all the mundane ways any of us might perish, from unpreventable accidents to deceptively simple yet sometimes untreatable conditions. Yet rather than inciting more anxiety, the jesting tone and sturdy compactness of the lineation and stanzaic structure come to feel almost reassuring. The poem further clarifies what medicine only deigns to acknowledge, that relief at being cured is always complicated by disbelief and fear of recurrence or relapse. Even as its ironic humor exposes the illusion that supposedly restored health somehow guarantees safety, that entirely familiar, if somewhat silly, initial human reaction, simultaneously but more pointedly critiqued is medicine’s hubris to even suggest such immunity. Perhaps this witty yet sobering poem helps us all to reflect on natural and ultimately inevitable death, which even the most clever medicine cannot cure.

item.title: Weight Loss in Older Adults With Persistent Atrial Fibrillation
item.description: To the Editor In the LOSE-AF randomized clinical trial, a low-calorie diet and behavioral support program achieved significant weight loss but did not improve atrial fibrillation (AF) symptoms, AF burden, or subsequent rhythm-control outcomes in older patients with persistent AF. We believe an imbalance in baseline rhythm-control therapies may have affected the interpretation of these null findings.

item.title: Weight Loss in Older Adults With Persistent Atrial Fibrillation
item.description: To the Editor In LOSE-AF, which investigated dietary weight loss in older patients with overweight and persistent AF, the intervention achieved significant weight loss (−9.7%) yet demonstrated no improvements in AF symptoms, AF burden, or cardiac remodeling. We would like to discuss several methodological limitations that warrant caution when interpreting the trial’s null findings.

item.title: Weight Loss in Older Adults With Persistent Atrial Fibrillation—Reply
item.description: In Reply We thank the correspondents for their interest in the LOSE-AF trial. LOSE-AF showed that in older patients with overweight and persistent AF, a low-calorie diet and behavioral support program was associated with significant weight loss at 8 months with no safety concerns but did not affect AF symptoms, AF burden, cardiac remodeling, or need for further rhythm control interventions.

item.title: The Next Decade of Health Spending
item.description: This Perspective discusses health care spending in the US and how factors such as consolidation, intensity of health care delivery, and artificial intelligence can affect who bears the costs and whether health gains are achieved.

item.title: A Future Without Excess Health Care Spending Growth?
item.description: This Perspective discusses various drivers of reductions in health care spending growth, including increasing use of artificial intelligence, expansion of value-based specialty care, and reductions in risk adjustment overpayment.

item.title: Idiopathic Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus: A Review
item.description: This Review discusses the pathophysiology, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical presentation, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis of idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus.

item.title: Initial Oxygen for Moderate- to Late-Preterm Infants
item.description: Each year, approximately 3.6 million infants are born in the US, approximately 10% of whom are preterm (less than 37 weeks’ gestation). For all newborns, successful transition from fetal to extrauterine life requires replacement of placental gas exchange with effective pulmonary respiration, a process that may falter in the absence of adequate lung aeration, surfactant function, and respiratory drive. Contemporary multicenter registry data indicate that up to 16% of all neonates and approximately half of infants born moderate to late preterm (32 to 36 weeks 6 days’ gestation) receive delivery room respiratory support to facilitate this transition, often including administration of supplemental oxygen. Concerns regarding the short- and long-term adverse effects associated with hypoxia and hyperoxia have motivated a long-standing focus on identifying the optimal initial fraction of inspired oxygen (Fio2) for use during immediate postnatal resuscitation.

item.title: Oxygen vs Air at Birth for Moderate- to Late-Preterm Infants
item.description: This cluster randomized clinical trial examines the safety and efficacy outcomes of starting respiratory support with a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.30 vs 0.21 among neonates born at 32 to 35 weeks’ gestation.

item.title: Oxygen vs Air at Birth for Moderate- to Late-Preterm Infants Research Summary
item.description: This study aimed to determine whether starting resuscitation with a fraction of inspired oxygen (Fio2) of 0.30 vs 0.21 for moderate- to late-preterm infants reduces ongoing respiratory support when leaving the delivery room.

item.title: Diagnosis of Celiac Disease
item.description: This Insights discusses the diagnosis of celiac disease, including biopsy confirmation vs serology-based diagnosis, in children and adults.

item.title: Patient Information: Celiac Disease
item.description: This JAMA Patient Page describes common symptoms, risk factors, screening tests, diagnosis, and treatment of celiac disease.

item.title: Initial HIV Therapy for Adults and Treatment-Associated Weight Gain
item.description: This randomized clinical trial compares the effects of a regimen with doravirine, lamivudine, and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate vs a regimen with dolutegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide on weight gain and viral suppression in adults with HIV without prior exposure to antiretroviral therapy.

item.title: Initial HIV Therapy for Adults and Treatment-Associated Weight Gain Research Summary
item.description: This trial investigated whether a regimen with doravirine, lamivudine, and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (DOR, 3TC, and TDF) would result in less weight gain compared with dolutegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide (DTG, FTC, and TAF) while maintaining similar HIV viral suppression.
